# Diagnosing a No-Start Condition on a 2003 Suzuki Katana 600

When a motorcycle that ran perfectly last week suddenly refuses to turn over, the diagnostic process often feels like searching for a needle in a haystack. The specific symptoms you are describingâa new battery confirming good electrical power, the starter motor audibly engaging, but the engine failing to rotate or completing a cycleânarrow down the problem significantly. You aren't fighting a dead battery or a seized crankshaft; the issue lies within the ignition timing, fuel delivery, or compression integrity.

The fact that the bike ran for approximately four seconds before dying initially suggests a failure in one of the three essential elements of combustion: air, fuel, or spark. Since you now have no rotation at all, the problem has likely escalated from an intermittent misfire to a complete system lockout. On a 2003 Suzuki Katana 600, the most probable culprit is a failure in the ignition system, specifically related to the CDI unit or the crankshaft position sensor (CKP).

The Katana utilizes a digital ignition system where the CDI (Capacitor Discharge Ignition) module controls the spark timing. If the CKP sensor fails or loses its connection, the ECU cannot detect when the piston is at top dead center. Without this signal, the CDI will not fire the spark plugs. This explains why you hear the starter motor turning the engine over (the mechanical action), but the engine never "takes over" because there is no ignition event to initiate combustion.

Before replacing expensive components like the CDI unit, verify the sensor and wiring integrity. The CKP sensor is typically located near the flywheel housing. Check for corrosion on the connector pins, a common issue after exposure to moisture or road salts. If the connector is clean but the bike still won't start, you may need to test for continuity with a multimeter or inspect for physical damage to the wiring harness that runs through the heat shield.

Fuel delivery is another critical area to investigate, even if the engine isn't turning over smoothly. The fuel pump on this model is often integrated into the tank assembly. If the fuel shut-off valve (solenoid) has failed in the closed position, no fuel will reach the carburetor or injection system. However, given your description of "trying to turn over," it is more likely a spark issue than a fuel starvation issue, as the engine usually requires a specific amount of crankshaft speed to engage the starter solenoid fully if there is backpressure from the carbs.

If you have verified the battery voltage and confirmed the starter motor is physically spinning the flywheel without resistance, consider checking the primary ignition coil. A weak coil might not generate enough spark under load, though this usually results in a misfire rather than a complete no-start. The transition from running for four seconds to zero rotation strongly points toward a timing signal loss.

In scenarios where the engine turns over but does not fire, always rule out compression issues caused by a blown head gasket or a stuck valve, though these are less likely to cause an immediate stop after a week of normal operation. The most efficient path forward is often to inspect the ignition kill switch and the neutral safety switch. Ensure the clutch lever is engaged if your Katana requires it to start, as many models have a safety interlock that prevents spark generation unless the clutch is pulled in or the gear selector is in neutral.

If all sensors and switches check out clean, the CDI unit itself may have failed internally. This component contains capacitors and transistors that degrade over time due to heat cycles. Replacing it is often more cost-effective than rebuilding the entire ignition system, but ensure you verify the secondary side (spark plugs and wires) before committing to the swap.
